title: What the US midterm elections mean for energy | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Ed Crooks argues the Democratic midterm wins will change little in US energy policy near term because of Trump's veto and executive powers, with change requiring bipartisan deals on permitting reform and data-centre electricity costs. Voter backlash against data centres is the most concrete shift, and a possible 2028 Democratic agenda (IRA 2.0, windfall tax, LNG export scrutiny) is flagged as longer-term risk.

insights.claim: Despite Democrats becoming the largest party in both the Senate and House, little will change in US energy policy when the new Congress is seated because Trump can veto legislation and Democrats will lack the two-thirds majorities needed to override.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Do not price a sharp US energy policy swing from the midterms; bipartisan deals are the only route to legislation.

insights.claim: Trump retains the ability to implement his agenda through regulations and executive actions, as his tariff strategy and the Middle East conflict were pursued without formal Congressional support.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Executive-branch action remains the main source of US energy policy risk.

insights.claim: The most significant constraint on Trump's actions is likely to be increased scrutiny from Democrat-controlled Congressional committees running their own investigations.

insights.so_what: Expect headline and oversight risk for administration energy actions rather than reversals.

insights.speaker: Ed Crooks

insights.claim: Permitting reform is the most important issue for the US energy industry in Congress right now, and the bipartisan BAAJA bill is due for a vote this week.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A near-term binary catalyst for pipelines, transmission and wind developers.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie analysts believe permitting reform close to the BAAJA form could materially shorten development timelines for oil and gas pipelines, power transmission lines and wind farms.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Passage would benefit pipeline, grid and wind project economics by cutting time and cost.

insights.claim: BAAJA won bipartisan backing by compromising between oil and gas and low-carbon interests, but is attacked from both sides, and some Democrats suggest withholding support to seek a better deal next year while others see it as the best available deal with Trump's support.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Passage this year is uncertain; delay risks a different bill in 2027.

themes.theme: Data centre backlash and electricity costs

insights.claim: Of 41 data-centre-related ballot proposals across 13 states, voters backed restrictions on development in 40.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Strong public opposition raises siting and approval risk for data-centre buildout and the associated power demand forecasts.
insights.quote: There were 41 proposals related to data centres on the ballot in 13 states, and on 40 of those a majority of voters backed restrictions on development.
insights.locator: Nearly everywhere they were given the option

insights.claim: Opposition to uncontrolled data-centre development is bipartisan, with Republican governors Ron DeSantis of Florida and Greg Abbott of Texas also announcing restrictions.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Restrictions are not a partisan swing risk; they persist across political control.
insights.locator: Candidates who spoke out against data centres

insights.claim: Texas, which has more proposed new data-centre capacity than any other state, will have Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who wants to extend Abbott's pause on new approvals and require data centres to cover their grid costs, while letting projects already under construction continue.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Texas data-centre pipeline faces delay and added cost allocation; under-construction projects are protected.
insights.locator: There has been particular interest in Texas

insights.claim: The Ratepayer Protection Act, which passed the House overwhelmingly in September, would require state regulators to consider standards forcing new data centres to cover the full cost of supporting grid and generation, while the GRID Savings Act would go further with a national mandate enforced through FERC rules.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Cost-causation rules would raise the all-in cost of data-centre power and shift costs from residential customers.
insights.locator: The proposed Ratepayer Protection Act was passed

insights.claim: Trump is likely to be reluctant to impose burdens on the AI industry because he strongly supports advanced AI as an economic and national security priority, so a compromise on data centres and electricity bills is likely to be negotiated next year.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Expect watered-down federal data-centre cost rules rather than strict mandates.
insights.locator: However, the president is also a strong supporter

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's Moderated Demand scenario models tighter data-centre restrictions, worsening grid-connection delays and continued equipment shortages, and still shows significant data-centre demand growth, only slower than the base case.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Even downside policy cases keep data-centre load growing, tempering both bull and bear power demand narratives.

insights.claim: Trump identified immigration law reform as a priority for working with Democrats, which depending on its structure could ease growing skills shortages for energy and other infrastructure projects.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Labour constraints on grid and energy buildout could ease if reform passes.

insights.claim: Renewable industry leaders want any future tax framework to be durable, since banks and investors gain confidence if taxes and regulations stay stable across administrations, which requires bipartisan support, after the IRA's key provisions were repealed by Republicans following its Democrat-only passage.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Policy whiplash raises the cost of capital for renewables; bipartisan-backed credits are more bankable.

insights.claim: Tax incentives serving bipartisan goals, such as the 45X advanced manufacturing credits, are most likely to be strengthened under a future Democratic government.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Domestic manufacturing credits are the safest policy-supported segment.

insights.claim: The Thriving Economy Project proposes a strategic energy affordability reserve funded by a windfall tax on oil and gas profits, which Crooks judges likely to be among the most controversial proposals, since taxing the industry could hit production and work against lowering fuel costs.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A 2028 windfall-tax risk for oil and gas producers is a tail risk, not a base case.

insights.claim: The industry consensus, shared by Wood Mackenzie analysts, is that energy export controls would be counter-productive and raise costs for American consumers; the Trump administration evaluated them as fuel prices surged this year but imposed none.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Export restrictions are unlikely to be imposed, supporting US LNG and product export volumes.

insights.claim: Democrats on the Thriving Economy Project propose an energy price safety valve to temporarily constrain exports of LNG, gasoline, diesel and heating oil, plus checks that new LNG projects would not raise consumer costs before approval.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Raises regulatory risk for new US LNG export approvals under a future Democratic administration.

insights.claim: The Biden administration's 2024 LNG export review found modelled residential prices in 2050 rising only 7% in the low gas supply scenario and 4% in the middle scenario, but those estimates predate the latest projections of strong US gas demand for power generation, which could amplify LNG's impact.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: The old evidence base for LNG export approvals is outdated, strengthening the case for tighter scrutiny.

insights.claim: Gas-fired data-centre self-generation can still push up gas prices and in turn power prices, so the Thriving Economy Project proposes mandating that all new data centres use renewables and energy storage.

insights.claim: The Thriving Economy Project argues wholesale power market reform was warranted even before the AI boom to encourage wind, solar and storage investment, and that data-centre demand makes it urgent, alongside a review of utility business models to prioritise affordability and cost-cutting incentives.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
